title: Does pick order matter for a robotic waste-sorting cell once items differ in value and arm travel?
lede: Follow-up to infra-sorting: with TACO's class mix, assumed item values (drink can = 4 plastic bottles) and 0.5 to 1.5 s of arm travel, picking the highest-value item first beats FIFO by only 0.1% at 1 item/m, 2.0% at 6/m and 4.8% at 10/m, and value-per-second picking matches it; belt speed and pick time matter far more than pick order.
summary: infra-sorting found that FIFO, LIFO and largest-first tie because every item had the same value, pick time and window. This project gives items a value by TACO category (assumed: a drink can is worth 4 plastic bottles, swept 1 to 16; glass 0.15) and a pick time of 0.5 to 1.5 s from lateral arm travel, and compares FIFO, highest-value-first and value-per-second dispatch on identical simulated arrival streams (40 runs, paired, 95 % intervals). Value-first beats FIFO by 0.1 % at 1 item/m, 0.6 % at 3, 2.0 % at 6 and 4.8 % at 10; the gain rises with can value (+1.1 % to +2.6 %), peaks for a mid-speed arm (0.6 m/s) and is near zero for a very slow or very fast one, and grows to +4.2 % when each contaminant costs two bottles. The two value-aware rules tie. Category values, arm speed, detector, grasp and reach are assumed (only can value and arm speed swept), the detector is not trained, and only greedy rules are tried, so this is no upper bound on dispatch gain; a real cell is not measured.
